Earlier, in Chapter XXXIX, paragraph 1, the text reads “It was the second week in May, in which the three young ladies set out together from Gracechurch-street” — Opening. In Chapter XLI, “Lydia will never be easy till she has exposed herself in some public place or other” (Chapter XLI, paragraph 15) — Mr. Bennet's acceptance. The father's failure to act sets up the crisis.

This passage (Chapter XLI, paragraph 22) develops women's limited choices: the story keeps returning to women's limited choices. Its words “uniformity” and “beauteous” carry that idea into this moment. The same concern returns in “She saw with the creative eye of fancy, the streets of that gay bathing place covered with officers.” (Chapter XLI, paragraph 22), so the two passages read as a pattern, not a single moment. Together they show the story treating women's limited choices as central.

This passage (Chapter XLI, paragraph 23) develops marriage and money: the story keeps returning to marriage and money. Its words “melancholy” and “conviction” carry that idea into this moment. The same concern returns in “On the very last day of the regiment’s remaining in Meryton, he dined with others of the officers at Longbourn; and so…” (Chapter XLI, paragraph 26), so the two passages read as a pattern, not a single moment. Together they show the story treating marriage and money as central.

Elizabeth's warning. The evidence is “Our importance, our respectability in the world, must be affected by the wild volatility” (Chapter XLI, paragraph 18). This develops family and reputation: the father's failure to act sets up the crisis. The words “respectability” and “volatility” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He admits "Lydia will never be easy till she has exposed herself," yet lets her go because "we shall have no peace at Longbourn" otherwise.
